chunks.section: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming k k -PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
chunks.text: Xinyu Luo 1 Jincheng Zhou 1 1 1 1 Department of Computer Science, Purdue University. Mengbo Wang 1,2 Zilin Shen 1 Nadia Atallah Lanman 2,3 Petros Drineas 1 Bruno Ribeiro 1 Brian Bullins 1 {luo466, zhou791, wang4887, shen624, natallah, pdrineas, ribeiro, bbullins}@purdue.edu † † thanks: Equal contribution.

A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

Training large language models (LLMs) under strict memory budgets has motivated a variety of low-rank optimization methods that restrict either the weights or the gradients to a low-dimensional subspace [ 10 , 39 , 20 ] . This broad field is primarily divided into two families. Weight-subspace methods , such as LoRA, adapt the model weights directly [ 10 , 14 ] . More recently, gradient-subspace methods , pioneered by GaLore [ 39 ] , project the gradients into a low-rank subspace before the optimizer step. The latter approach and its subsequent works have proven particularly effective, demonstrating superior memory savings and performance by focusing on the dynamics of the optimizer itself [ 39 , 38 , 14 , 8 , 5 , 28 ] . Yet most gradient-subspace methods in this promising family face a core technical challenge: that the principal gradient directions, instead of being static, evolve as the model weights are updated throughout training. Consequently, the success of any such method hinges on how effectively it adapts to this changing subspace. GaLore tackles this by periodically recomputing the entire subspace from scratch via an expensive SVD [ 39 ] , a process that acts as a “cold restart” and discards prior subspace information. More recent methods, such as Online Subspace Descent (OSD) [ 15 ] , move towards more continuous adaptation by using a secondary, non-convex optimization loop to “catch up” to the moving subspace.

Bottom-left corner is the ideal region. Ori ( ⋆ \star ) forms a better Pareto frontier, achieving a superior performance-to-memory trade-off compared to state-of-the-art baselines like GaLore ( ∘ \circ ) and OSD ( □ \square ). However, existing adaptation strategies may overlook a key empirical observation that we make explicit in this work: the gradient subspace does not jump erratically but, rather, drifts smoothly after warm-up. In other words, the projector at step t t is predictably close to that at t − Δ ​ t t-\Delta t for small Δ ​ t \Delta t (e.g., 20). This slow, structured drift suggests a different perspective. Rather than recomputing the subspace (as in GaLore [ 39 ] ) or optimizing it with non-convex gradient descent (as in OSD [ 15 ] ), we can track it with a streaming update that makes small, frequent rotations aligned with the most recent gradients, while also preserving and transferring optimizer statistics across these rotations. In light of these observations, we arrive at a different design problem: How do we continuously maintain a memory-light, compute-efficient, and stable projector that tracks a drifting gradient subspace?

We thus introduce Ori , a streaming k k -PCA-based O ja-style updated low- r ank i terative optimizer, designed to exploit the slow-drift regime of LLM gradient subspaces. Rather than treating each subspace estimation as an independent, “cold-start” problem—as is the case with periodic SVD recomputation in GaLore—Ori treats subspace estimation as a continuous tracking problem. The core innovation of Ori lies in its drift-aware bootstrapping mechanism: we carry over (transfer) the subspace basis from previous steps as the initialization state for the current step. Because of the slow-drift phenomenon, the prior basis provides a suitable starting point that requires only a few lightweight, streaming k k -PCA-inspired updates to realign with the instantaneous gradient geometry. In practice, Ori instantiates this via the Oja++ algorithm [ 24 , 1 ] , which enables high-frequency basis rotations at a per-step cost of only 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ k 2 ) \mathcal{O}(dk^{2}) . This approach allows for a warm-start transfer of Adam-style first and second moments between successive bases, ensuring stable optimization dynamics. Beyond computational efficiency, we show that this formulation allows Ori to achieve provable sublinear dynamic regret bounds under drift, providing new theoretical tools and guarantees for tracking fidelity that static recomputation methods lack.

Empirically, Ori narrowly tracks the evolving gradient subspace and converts this tracking fidelity into end-to-end wins where it matters most: very low ranks. Under tight rank budgets, each dimension in the projector is precious, and stale misalignment is especially costly. Empirical results show that Ori reduces the performance gap of state-of-the-art low-rank baselines to the full-rank Adam optimizer by up to 69.3% on the 1B LLaMA pre-training task, where the optimizer state rank is 128 in contrast to the model embedding dimension of 2048. And on Roberta-Base fine-tuning tasks, where the ranks are even lower (8 or 4), Ori achieves superior performance on 10 out of 16 scenarios. Moreover, Ori achieved this superior performance with one of the lowest computation budgets. See Figure 1 for a performance–memory overview on LLaMA-1B pre-training, where Ori consistently sits on the bottom-left frontier. Through ablation, we observe that (i) increasing the projector-update period degrades performance—quantifying the cost of staleness, and (ii) injecting a small carry-over (via a drift coefficient ρ ≈ 0.99 \rho\approx 0.99 ) improves accuracy—confirming the value of continuity and statistic transfer. Across pre-training and fine-tuning settings, Ori consistently improves the performance–memory trade-off over LoRA, GaLore, and OSD in the low-rank regime, thereby reducing the gap to full-rank Adam. Our primary contributions in this work are as follows: • We identify and quantify slow gradient subspace drift during LLM training and argue that exploiting its continuity – not merely reacting to it – matters for low-rank optimization.

• We propose Ori, a drift-aware low-rank optimizer that equips gap-free streaming k k -PCA with moment transfer to achieve continuous, high-frequency projector updates at negligible cost. • We provide theoretical support via new dynamic-regret bounds under drift, yielding sublinear regret in the noiseless setting with mild dependence on the consecutive drift parameter. • We present empirical results showing Ori’s superior performance under stringent rank constraints, with ablations isolating the roles of update frequency and drift-aware continuity.
We refer the reader to Appendix B for a more detailed discussion of related work.

Low-rank optimization in LLMs can be broadly divided into two categories. Weight-subspace methods adapt the model weights by constraining them to a low-rank manifold, a paradigm popularized by LoRA and its many variants [ 10 , 14 , 37 , 20 , 8 ] . In contrast, Ori belongs to the second category, gradient-subspace methods , which operate on a low-rank projection of the gradients. This line of work was pioneered by GaLore [ 39 ] , which uses periodic Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify and project gradients onto a low-rank basis. Many subsequent works have built upon this foundation by incorporating diverse strategies such as quantization [ 38 ] , structured sparsity [ 22 ] , random projections [ 9 , 32 ] , and importance sampling [ 36 , 16 ] . However, a common limitation underlines these approaches: by relying on static or infrequently updated projectors, they are inherently reactive to the evolving gradient landscape. This can lead to a “staleness penalty,” where gradients are projected onto an outdated basis, losing critical information for optimization. Ori is designed to directly counteract this penalty by replacing infrequent recomputation with a continuous, online tracking mechanism.

The challenge of staleness in subspace projection has motivated online methods that update projectors frequently without relying on full SVD. Recent work explores auxiliary optimization techniques for dynamic subspace learning [ 15 , 23 , 28 , 27 ] . Nguyen and Nguyen [23] propose Subset-Norm and Subspace-Momentum, which decouples optimization by applying momentum in a low-dimensional subspace while performing SGD in the orthogonal complement. Robert et al. [28] use block power iteration on a weighted gradient-EMA combination to adapt optimizer states to evolving subspaces. Rajabi et al. [27] track subspaces on the Grassmannian manifold via geodesic updates, leveraging past estimates and error feedback for accuracy. Liang et al. [15] propose a robust procedure using a secondary optimizer to perform gradient descent directly on the subspace manifold, initialized from the previous projector.

Ori adopts a fundamentally distinct strategy. Rather than relying on a secondary optimizer, it leverages the streaming k k -PCA algorithm, Oja++ [ 1 ] , to update the projector. This distinction carries significant implications. First, gradient descent on the subspace manifold is inherently non-convex and complex, but Oja-style multiplicative updates come with strong theoretical assurances. Specifically, Oja++ achieves a provably “gap-free” convergence rate, offering greater robustness in static settings compared to gradient-based methods. Second, as formalized in our theoretical contributions, our Oja-based update exhibits desirable properties even in non-stationary, drifting environments, yielding strong dynamic regret bounds. Finally, the Oja++ update is computationally cheaper than gradient descent on the manifold, enabling Ori to update the projector more frequently. This higher frequency allows for improved tracking of the evolving gradient landscape.

In this section, we further discuss the technical foundation of Ori. First, we establish and quantify the problem of gradient subspace drift, highlighting the limitations of existing approaches. Next, we introduce the core motivation of bootstrapping subspace updates, which forms the conceptual basis of our method. We then detail the specific online algorithm, a modified Oja++, used to implement this solution. Finally, we present the complete Ori algorithm, synthesizing these components into a cohesive and efficient optimization procedure.

Low-rank optimizers that rely on periodic updates, such as GaLore [ 39 ] , implicitly assume that the principal gradient subspace remains relatively stable between updates. With the subspace overlap metric established, we empirically tested the stability assumption by measuring the overlap (with Δ ​ t = 10 \Delta t=10 ) throughout the pre-training of a 60M LLaMA model via the Adam optimizer on the C4 dataset (further experiment details can be found in Appendix E ). The results, shown in Figure 2 , provide clear evidence for a “slow drift” hypothesis. After an initial transient phase, the average gradient subspace overlap across all tested ranks ( k ∈ { 8 , 32 , 128 } k\in\{8,32,128\} ) stabilizes at a high value between 0.55 and 0.75. Crucially, this is significantly higher than the overlap observed for random subspaces of the same rank, confirming the existence of meaningful temporal structure. This indicates: (i) The static subspace assumption is false , as the overlap is consistently below 1.0, and the change over just 10 steps is substantial. (ii) The evolution is not erratic , as the overlap remains remarkably stable, suggesting the subspace moves with a predictable “velocity” rather than teleporting randomly. (iii) The phenomenon is fundamental , as the stable drift is present across a range of ranks, suggesting it is an intrinsic property of the optimization trajectory. This temporal coherence is precisely the property that an online tracking algorithm can exploit.

chunks.text: While Equation 2 and Equation 3 form the conceptual basis, we specifically employ a more robust variant, Oja++ [ 1 ] , for its crucial theoretical advantage of gap-free convergence . This means its convergence rate is independent of the eigengap (the difference between consecutive singular values of the gradient covariance matrix), a property vital for LLM training where such gaps can be small. The bootstrapping technique applies directly to Oja++ as well: the previous basis Q t − 1 Q_{t-1} serves as the warm start for the multi-stage Oja++ update. This combination of a theoretically sound, gap-free algorithm with a drift-aware bootstrapping strategy gives rise to the full form of our proposed optimizer, Ori, whose core projector update routine is detailed in Algorithm 1 . For the algorithm pseudocode of Ori with AdamW, we refer the readers to Algorithm 2 in Appendix C . In particular, we provide an amortized runtime complexity analysis of Ori in Appendix C.3 .

To demonstrate that the design principles behind Ori can be applied to specialized, state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers other than GaLore, we examine LDAdam [ 28 ] . LDAdam enhances the standard Adam optimizer by employing a projection-aware, momentum-based update alongside a generalized error-feedback mechanism. This design aligns with findings from MicroAdam [ 21 ] , which showed that applying error feedback at every iteration is essential for recovering Adam-like convergence at million- and billion-parameter scales (e.g., BERT/LLaMA). These techniques significantly enhance language model pre-training performance in extremely low-rank settings (e.g., rank 32 with an embedding size of 2048). However, LDAdam faces a critical barrier to practical deployment: it requires updating the projector at every training step ( T = 1 T=1 ) to maintain performance, incurring prohibitive computational costs. As shown in our later empirical results ( Table 2 ), when the update interval is increased to T = 200 T=200 – matching the standard schedule of GaLore – LDAdam’s performance degrades significantly. We attribute this drop to LDAdam’s reliance on a simple single-step power iteration method for subspace estimation, which we hypothesize is insufficient for tracking the drifting gradient subspace over large update intervals. Inspired by Ori, we introduce a multi-step stochastic power iteration mechanism into LDAdam’s update routine. We refer to this improved optimizer as O-LDAdam, reflecting its infusion of Ori’s online subspace tracking into LDAdam’s error-correcting framework. We provide further algorithmic details in Appendix D .

We aim to demonstrate that Ori: (i) achieves superior performance against existing low-rank optimizers in both pre-training and fine-tuning, particularly under extremely low rank scenarios; (ii) improves memory and computational efficiency; and (iii) derives its benefits from its core design principles, as shown through ablation studies.

We evaluate Ori against a consistent set of state-of-the-art optimizers, all built upon the Adam optimizer. For each baseline, we adopt the hyperparameter configurations recommended in their respective original publications and official codebases. Full experimental details are provided in Appendix E . Our baselines include: Full-Rank Adam , the standard optimizer serving as a practical upper bound on performance (using default β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999 , and ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} ); Weight-Subspace Methods , represented by LoRA [ 10 ] for fine-tuning (with a LoRA alpha of 32 and a dropout of 0.05) and its pre-training variant ReLoRA [ 14 ] (with optimizer states reset every 1000 steps and no full-rank warmup); and Gradient-Subspace Methods . This category includes GaLore [ 39 ] , which employs periodic SVD (update frequency T = 200 T=200 ; pre-training scale α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 ; fine-tuning scale α ∈ { 2 , 4 } \alpha\in\{2,4\} ), and OSD (Online Subspace Descent) [ 15 ] , another state-of-the-art method that performs gradient descent directly on the subspace manifold (similarly using T = 200 T=200 , pre-training α = 0.25 \alpha=0.25 , and fine-tuning α ∈ { 2 , 4 } \alpha\in\{2,4\} ). Finally, LDAdam [ 28 ] , which update its projection matrix via power iteration, alongside orthogonal techniques such as an error feedback mechanism and momentum-based state updates. Although the original LDAdam was designed exclusively for most frequent per-step updates ( T = 1 T=1 ), for the purpose of this work, we adapted it also to the efficient delayed update setting ( T = 200 T=200 ). We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

To test the generality of our subspace tracking approach, we benchmarked against LDAdam, a stronger baseline that utilizes error feedback and momentum buffering. While LDAdam achieves impressive performance when updating the projector at every step ( T = 1 T=1 ), this comes at a high computational cost. As shown in Table 2, simply increasing the update interval to T = 200 T=200 (matching GaLore’s efficiency) causes LDAdam’s performance to collapse (e.g., perplexity spikes from 20.27 to 45.66 on LLaMA-1B at r = 32 r=32 ). However, by replacing LDAdam’s simple power iteration with our stochastic power iteration (O-LDAdam), we effectively bridge this gap. O-LDAdam ( T = 200 T=200 ) not only recovers the performance of the expensive LDAdam ( T = 1 T=1 ) baseline but frequently surpasses it in extremely low-rank regimes. Notably, on the 1B model at rank 32, O-LDAdam achieves a perplexity of 15.66, significantly outperforming the vanilla LDAdam ( T = 1 T=1 ) score of 20.27, all while maintaining the computationally efficient T = 200 T=200 schedule. This confirms that the subspace tracking principles of Ori are orthogonal to error-feedback mechanisms and can be composed to create state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers.

To evaluate Ori’s effectiveness on adaptation tasks, we fine-tuned a RoBERTa-Base model on the GLUE benchmark [ 31 ] . For each task, we report the mean and standard deviation of task-specific metrics over three runs with different random seeds. Further details on evaluation metrics are provided in Appendix E . The fine-tuning results in Table 3 underscore Ori’s prominent performance. Across both rank settings, Ori achieves the highest average score among all low-rank methods. At rank-8, Ori’s average score of 86.30 not only surpasses GaLore (84.34) and LoRA (79.68) but also exceeds the full-rank Adam baseline (85.82). This strong performance continues at rank-4, where Ori (85.61) again leads all low-rank optimizers except for LDAdam with T = 1 T=1 . In particular, Ori achieves the top score in 10 out of the 16 total task/rank combinations. Its particularly strong advantage on challenging tasks like CoLA (63.58 vs. GaLore’s 58.24 at r=8) further validates its robustness and demonstrates that its drift-aware optimization is highly effective for both pre-training and adaptation tasks.

chunks.section: Impact of the Drift Coefficient ( ρ \rho ).
chunks.text: We first analyze the effect of the drift coefficient ρ \rho , which controls how much of the previous step’s projector is carried over to initialize the current step’s projector. As shown in Figure 3(a) , we observe a clear and consistent trend across all ranks: a value of ρ = 0.99 \rho=0.99 yields the best performance. This has two key implications. First, the significant performance drop at ρ = 0.0 \rho=0.0 (a fully random restart) corroborates our central claim that transferring information about the previous subspace is crucial for effective optimization. Second, the slight performance dip at ρ = 1.0 \rho=1.0 (a direct carryover with no noise) suggests that injecting a small amount of randomness is a beneficial regularization strategy. Overall, we choose ρ = 0.99 \rho=0.99 for Ori in all pre-training and fine-tuning.

chunks.section: Impact of Projector Update Frequency ( T T )
chunks.text: We test our hypothesis that frequent, lightweight updates are superior to infrequent, heavy ones by varying the update period from 10 to 200 (which matches GaLore’s recommended schedule [ 39 ] ). As shown in Figure 3(b) , more frequent updates consistently lead to lower loss (better performance). This phenomenon is especially prominent in the extremely low-rank setting ( r = 8 r=8 ), where the cost of using a stale projector is most severe. This finding contrasts sharply with the ablation results from GaLore [ 39 ] , in which the authors reported no benefit from more frequent GaLore SVD updates. We hypothesize this is a unique advantage of Ori: because GaLore’s periodic SVD acts as a “cold restart” that does not carry over subspace statistics, frequent updates may not be as beneficial. In contrast, since Ori is explicitly designed to track subspace drift, it can effectively leverage more frequent updates to maintain a higher-fidelity representation of the gradient landscape. For our main experiments, we set T = 20 T=20 , as it strikes an effective balance between model performance and computational overhead.

To empirically justify choosing Oja++, we compare the performance of Oja++ against the standard Oja algorithm as the subroutine for updating the gradient projector. The results in Figure 3(c) are unequivocal: Oja++ consistently outperforms standard Oja across all tested ranks. This aligns with prior theoretical work showing Oja++ has a provably better convergence rate in static streaming k k -PCA settings [ 1 ] . Our results provide new empirical evidence that this advantage extends to the dynamic, non-stationary environment of LLM training, where Oja++’s superior tracking ability translates directly to better model performance.
Finally, aside from the theoretical runtime complexity analysis in Appendix C.3 , we provide an empirical memory and computation time comparison in Appendix F.1 .

We introduced Ori, a drift-aware low-rank optimizer that continuously tracks the gradient subspace with streaming k k -PCA and preserves optimizer statistics across projector updates, mitigating staleness while keeping memory and compute low. Across theory (dynamic-regret under drift) and experiments, Ori consistently narrows the gap to full-rank training in the extremely low-rank regime while remaining faster and more memory-efficient than prior gradient-projection methods. We discuss limitations of our work and directions for future research, including behavior under heterogeneous training data and explicit optimizer state rotation across basis changes, in Appendix G .

chunks.section: Parameter weights subspace projection based descent.
chunks.text: Recent research has explored learned subspace descent methods, where gradient updates are confined to a low-dimensional subspace of the model’s weights that is itself learned during training. A straightforward instance is to parameterize each weight matrix as a product of low-rank factors (e.g. W = B ​ A W=BA with B ∈ ℝ m × r , A ∈ ℝ r × n B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},A\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times n} ) and optimize those factors via gradient descent [ 10 , 11 , 18 ] . While such plain low-rank factorization can significantly reduce parameters, it often falls short of full-rank performance [ 39 ] , prompting more adaptive approaches. ReLoRA [ 14 ] tackles this by periodically absorbing the learned low-rank updates into the main weights and introducing new factor matrices, gradually increasing the effective rank of W W over training to recover expressiveness. SLTrain [ 8 ] takes a complementary route by representing each weight as the sum of a trainable low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix ( W = B ​ A + S W=BA+S ) and jointly optimizing both; this hybrid decomposition boosts model capacity while still confining updates to a learned low-dimensional (and partially sparse) subspace. Other methods learn to adjust the subspace itself: AdaLoRA [ 37 ] dynamically adapts the rank of the low-rank adapters based on an importance metric (simulating SVD pruning of negligible directions), effectively learning the most productive subspace basis during training. Likewise, LORO [ 20 ] directly optimizes the model on a low-rank manifold (using Riemannian optimization), ensuring all gradient steps stay within a trainable low-dimensional parameter space. Beyond pure low-rank factors, structured subspace strategies have been proposed: BTT [ 25 ] introduces a block tensor train factorization (via Kronecker-product structured weight matrices) with the factor components learned by gradient descent, and CoMERA [ 34 ] reshapes weight matrices into higher-order tensors that are decomposed into smaller learned tensors, enforcing a compact learned subspace of parameters. All of these approaches maintain that the projection basis (e.g. the low-rank factors or tensor components) is updated by training, allowing the subspace to evolve to fit the data.

chunks.section: Parameter weights subspace projection based descent.
chunks.text: In contrast, other methods restrict gradient descent to a fixed or partially fixed subspace of the weights, where the projection basis remains static (or changes only via non-gradient steps) for some duration. SwitchLoRA [ 40 ] exemplifies this paradigm by using LoRA-style low-rank adapters but periodically switching their basis vectors (columns of B B or rows of A A ) with new ones during training, instead of continuously refining the same basis. This schedule of refreshing the adapter subspace (inspired by ReLoRA’s rank-growth idea) lets the model incrementally cover diverse low-dimensional subspaces without explicitly learning the basis via backpropagation. Similarly, LoQT [ 17 ] employs a fixed-basis approach for efficiency: it initializes each weight with two low-rank factors W ≈ B ​ A W\approx BA , then freezes one factor (keeping it constant and even quantized to save memory) and only trains the other factor B B . Periodically, the product B ​ A BA is added into the full weight matrix W W (and possibly B B is reinitialized), but the subspace defined by the fixed factor A A remains unchanged during those intervals. By operating in a predetermined low-rank subspace (or a sequence of static subspaces), SwitchLoRA and LoQT avoid the overhead of learning new basis directions, instead confining updates to coefficient adjustments within a fixed projector. This ensures that gradient descent explores a low-dimensional slice of the parameter space defined a priori (or piecewise fixed), in contrast to the above methods that co-learn the subspace itself during training.

Recent research has explored gradient subspace projection descent methods to reduce memory and computation by restricting updates to a low-dimensional subspace. GaLore [ 39 ] pioneered this approach, using SVD to project each gradient onto a top- r r singular vector subspace. This low-rank update dramatically lowers memory usage for gradients and optimizer states. Numerous extensions build on GaLore’s foundation. Fira [ 2 ] adds an orthogonal complement term to reintroduce full-rank gradient information, closing the performance gap to full Adam without extra memory. Natural GaLore [ 4 ] integrates natural gradient preconditioning into GaLore’s update, while Q-GaLore [ 38 ] combines low-rank projection with low-bit quantization for further memory savings. Other variants modify how the subspace is selected. COAP [ 33 ] learns a correlation-aware projection matrix for improved efficiency, and GRASS [ 22 ] constructs sparse projection bases guided by gradient row norms to accelerate training. FRUGAL [ 41 ] performs an Adam-style update in the projected subspace and a simultaneous SGD step on the orthogonal complement, enabling updates across the full parameter space with minimal extra memory overhead. Tensor-GaLore [ 6 ] extends the low-rank projection principle to higher-order tensor parameters (beyond flat matrices), broadening applicability while preserving memory benefits.

We frame the phenomenon of gradient subspace drift within the broader theoretical context of concept drift in online learning. Foundational work in this area establishes regret guarantees for learners adapting to a slowly shifting target distribution [ 3 ] . This theoretical lens is highly relevant to LLM training, where empirical evidence shows that gradients concentrate in a low-dimensional, slowly evolving subspace [ 7 , 12 ] . While the idea of a shifting target is well-established, our work is the first to formally analyze a low-rank optimizer through the framework of dynamic regret under concept drift. This provides a principled theoretical foundation for Ori’s performance and differentiates it from prior methods that focused primarily on algorithmic or empirical contributions.

Meanwhile, some works address the computational cost of maintaining the subspace or explore dynamic subspace strategies. Galore+ [ 16 ] reduces SVD overhead by performing the decomposition on only a randomly chosen component (e.g. one attention head) per update, significantly speeding up training at the cost of a slight approximation error. SubTrack-Grad [ 27 ] and Online Subspace Descent [ 15 ] both dynamically update the projection basis: they solve auxiliary optimization problems (e.g. least-squares fits) to adjust the subspace so that it continues to approximate the current gradient well over time. In contrast, Flora [ 32 ] and GoLore [ 9 ] propose using fixed random projections of gradients, achieving memory savings with competitive performance to GaLore but without expensive SVD computations. I3S [ 36 ] introduces an importance sampling subspace selection scheme, weighting basis directions by their singular values to adaptively refine GaLore’s subspace and further improve convergence. Finally, the recent GaLore 2 framework [ 30 ] addresses practical challenges like SVD cost and parallelization integration (e.g. with FSDP), and demonstrates the scalability of subspace-projected training by pre-training a 7B-parameter LLM with up to 500B tokens using significantly less memory.

chunks.section: Online k-PCA subspace descent related method.
chunks.text: Recent optimizers exploit low-dimensional subspaces to reduce memory cost in large-scale training via online k k -PCA. For example, Subspace-Momentum confines the momentum vector to a fixed k k -dimensional subspace (e.g., spanned by top singular directions) while performing standard SGD in the orthogonal complement, substantially lowering optimizer-state memory and admitting high-probability convergence guarantees under standard conditions [ 23 ] . The subspace can be chosen once or periodically refreshed via streaming singular vectors (e.g., computing top- k k components every G G steps) to adapt to evolving gradients [ 23 ] . Similarly, Online Subspace Descent forgoes expensive SVD-based updates by continuously adapting the projection matrix through an online k k -PCA algorithm [ 15 ] . This approach provides a convergence guarantee for arbitrary subspace update rules in such low-rank optimizers and maintains an up-to-date basis with minimal overhead, eliminating full SVD computations during training [ 15 ] . Applied to LLM pre-training, the online subspace optimizer achieves lower perplexity than prior low-rank methods and narrows the performance gap to full-rank training on benchmarks [ 15 ] .

A growing body of work indicates that SGD dynamics concentrate in a low-dimensional, slowly evolving subspace, motivating algorithms that explicitly track or exploit subspace drift during training. Theory shows: (i) gradient updates lie within a tiny active subspace, suggesting that learning can be captured by a small set of dominant directions [ 7 ] ; (ii) online learning with concept drift admits regret guarantees against a slowly shifting comparator, formalizing performance when the target (or optimal subspace) moves over time [ 3 ] ; and (iii) low-dimensional training succeeds once the subspace dimension exceeds a threshold tied to the loss landscape’s Gaussian width, explaining why few degrees of freedom can suffice and how this threshold depends on initialization [ 12 ] . On the practical side for large-scale LLMs, recent methods instantiate drifting-subspace training by refreshing projection bases during optimization; among them, I3S [ 36 ] samples singular directions by importance to diversify consecutive subspaces, alleviating “frozen” dominant bases while retaining convergence guarantees comparable to random-projection methods and delivering stronger pretraining perplexity in practice. Together, these results motivate modeling—and algorithmically tracking—gradient subspace drift when designing memory-efficient, very low-rank training procedures for LLMs.

chunks.section: C.2 Ori Hyperparameters and Recommended Search Strategy
chunks.text: In total, Ori consists of the following 7 important hyperparameters, listed roughly in the order of the most to least influential to model performance as we observed during method development. • Scale γ \gamma : Similar to GaLore’s scale α \alpha [ 39 ] , this parameter effectively scales the actual learning rate for the model layers for which Ori project the gradients. We suggest always search over this parameter as it highly correlates with model performance. Empirically, we found that one can set a higher γ \gamma value in the extremely low rank settings, while smaller γ \gamma tend to yield more stable training at higher ranks. We suggest γ ∈ { 0.25 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 1.0 } \gamma\in\{0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\} for large model pre-training, and γ ∈ { 2.0 , 4.0 } \gamma\in\{2.0,4.0\} for very low-rank fine-tuning. • Drift coefficient ρ \rho : This parameter controls how much the last step’s projector is carried over to warm-start the next step’s projector Oja updates. A ρ = 0.0 \rho=0.0 means total random restart, and a ρ = 1.0 \rho=1.0 means total carry-over with no randomness injected. As established in Section 5.4 , the ρ = 0.99 \rho=0.99 tend to be the universally good setting. We also found that ρ ∈ { 0.8 , 0.9 } \rho\in\{0.8,0.9\} can be good alternatives in a few scenarios. • Projector update period T period T_{\text{period}} : This parameter controls the frequency of Ori’s update. As established in Section 5.4 , we suggest T period = 20 T_{\text{period}}=20 as it strikes a perfect balance between model performance and computation budget.

chunks.section: Appendix D Stochastic Power Iteration for LDAdam
chunks.text: LDAdam [ 28 ] is a memory-efficient variant of Adam for low-rank LLM training that performs adaptive updates inside a low-dimensional gradient subspace, while using projection-aware rules to transfer the first/second-moment states of Adam as the subspace changes over time. It computes the subspace via the warm-started block power iteration method (warm-started by SVD library call at the very first update step) and adds a generalized error-feedback mechanism to compensate for information lost when compressing both gradients and the first/second-moment optimizer states. As a result, it approaches Adam-like behavior with much smaller optimizer memory in the low-rank setting. A key practical limitation, however, is that LDAdam typically requires per-step projector updates (T=1) to maintain accuracy, which can be computationally prohibitive. On the other hand, naively increasing LDAdam’s subspace update interval to T = 200 T=200 – matching the standard schedule used by GaLore – causes a significant performance drop. This is shown in Table 2 , our main results for pretraining the Llama model on C4 dataset. In particular, on the largest, 1b-size model, we find that the training process under LDAdam with T = 200 T=200 may fail to converge, leading to very large evaluation perplexity (above 160 perplexity for both rank r = 512 r=512 and r = 128 r=128 ). We attribute this sensitivity and instability to LDAdam’s reliance on a single-step full-block power-iteration-style refresh: when the gradient subspace drifts over long intervals (e.g., T = 200 T=200 ), a one-step update is often insufficient to re-align the projector.

We use the C4 dataset for the LLaMA model pre-training task. C4 dataset is a colossal, cleaned version of Common Crawl’s web crawl corpus, mainly intended for pre-training language models and word representations, available under the Open Data Commons Attribution License (ODC-BY) license [ 26 ] . We report the final validation perplexity (the lower the better) for the main experiment table ( Table 1 ). For all pre-training experiments, we adjust the gradient accumulation steps accordingly, depending on the available GPUs, so that the effective total batch size for all runs are 512 (for instance, an actual batch size of 64 with 8 gradient accumulation steps results in the effective batch size of 512). In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

We discuss several limitations of this work that present opportunities for future research.

Our empirical evaluation focuses on single-domain pretraining (the C4 dataset [ 26 ] ) and standard fine-tuning benchmarks (the GLUE dataset [ 31 ] ), following the established experimental protocol used by GaLore [ 39 ] , OSD [ 15 ] , and other gradient-subspace methods. An important open question, shared by the many works of low-rank optimizer research, is whether global gradient subspace projection methods perform well when training on highly heterogeneous data mixtures spanning diverse domains (e.g., code, mathematics, chat, and multilingual data simultaneously). In such settings, it is conceivable that the top- k k principal gradient directions could be dominated by the most prevalent domains, potentially suppressing rare but important domain-specific gradient signals. Recent work by Li et al. [13] suggests that gradient conflicts are minimal during large-scale LLM pretraining across multilingual and multi-domain settings, which provides initial evidence that this concern may be less severe than expected. Nevertheless, a rigorous investigation—including defining appropriate evaluation metrics for specialized capability retention, curating heterogeneous benchmarks, and systematically comparing low-rank methods under diverse data compositions—would be a valuable contribution to the field. Notably, Ori’s high-frequency streaming updates and potential easy composability with standard multi-task optimization methods (e.g., PCGrad [ 35 ] ) position it well for such settings, but empirical validation remains future work.

chunks.section: Optimizer state handling across basis changes.
chunks.text: When Ori updates the gradient projector P P via Oja++, the Adam optimizer moments M M and V V are not explicitly rotated into the new basis. Instead, Ori relies on the slow-drift property ( ρ = 0.99 \rho=0.99 ) and Adam’s exponential moving average to naturally decay stale moment information. While this is empirically effective (as validated by the high subspace overlap in Figure 2 and the strong end-to-end performance), explicitly projecting optimizer states across basis changes—as explored by Schotthöfer et al. [29] in the context of weight-space low-rank factorization—could yield further improvements, particularly in regimes with faster subspace drift or lower ρ \rho . We consider this a promising direction for future work.

Ori operates at a fixed rank r r throughout training, which must be specified in advance. Combining Ori’s streaming subspace tracking with rank-adaptive methods such as AdaLoRA [ 37 ] , which dynamically allocates rank budgets across layers based on importance metrics, could enable more flexible and efficient low-rank training. Since Ori’s subspace tracking mechanism is orthogonal to rank selection, such a combination is a natural extension.

This paper proposes a novel low-rank optimizer for training large language models, which is a foundational research area in machine learning. As such, we do not foresee any immediate negative societal impacts. However, we recognize that our work, like most AI research, could have broad, long-term implications, including potential issues with energy consumption or, indirectly, in downstream applications.
